title: Consumer and Multi-Market Products
summary: Consumer and multi-market product design addresses consumer-facing products that must operate across countries, languages, brands, distributors, and local usage conventions without fragmenting into unrelated local variants. The documented evidence includes Elsner Elektronik, OLX, Streetec, AIT, and visioncheckout examples, with each claim calibrated to the available evidence.
keyFacts: Consumer product design differs from professional software because users have not invested in learning the domain and compare responsiveness to smartphone experience.
The Elsner Elektronik Cala Touch KNX case involved a 4-inch round TFT LCD room controller at 480×480px, mounted at 140cm, with use across 54 countries.
Colle & Hiszem (2004) is cited for touch target sizing: minimum 13mm, with accuracy plateauing at approximately 22mm.

Elsner dealer prototype reviews produced 30 responses from dealers across 10 countries; 100% of responding dealers, 30 of 130 total dealers, rated the redesign as an improvement, client-reported from Elsner's dealer network.
The OLX automotive marketplace case produced a marketplace coherence framework for Poland, Portugal, and Romania; no user performance metrics were measured in that engagement.

bodySections.heading: Consumer and Multi-Market Product Design as a Creative Navy Context
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Consumer and multi-market product design is the design of consumer-facing or channel-mediated products that must remain coherent across markets while accommodating local behaviours, brands, languages, regulatory constraints, distributor feedback, and wide differences in user dexterity and technical familiarity.

The core design problem is controlled variation. A multi-market product needs enough local adaptation to fit real market conventions, but enough shared architecture for engineering, product, marketing, and support teams to maintain a coherent product.

bodySections.heading: Consumer Interfaces Must Support a Wide Accessibility Range
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Consumer product design differs from professional software because users have not invested in learning the domain. Users compare consumer devices against the responsiveness, clarity, and interaction quality of smartphones, even when the product is an embedded controller with constrained hardware.

The Elsner Elektronik Cala Touch KNX case illustrates this accessibility range. The product was a 4-inch round TFT LCD room controller at 480×480px, wall-mounted at 140cm, used to control heating, cooling, lighting, blinds, and scenes. It operated in the KNX building automation ecosystem across 54 countries.

The documented user split included tech-savvy building automation professionals and elderly consumers with limited dexterity, both using the same device in daily life. The KNX split also mattered: systems engineers configured the device through ETS, while occupants operated it daily without configuration access. Some interface patterns that appeared to be design decisions were actually workarounds for firmware or configuration constraints that occupants could not change.

The previous interface used carousel navigation with 1–10 pages and swipe-only access. A user could need up to 10 swipes to reach a function. The touch layer was laggy because of microcontroller processing limits, and the product felt unresponsive relative to smartphone standards. The consumer electronics comparison was structural: users experienced the difference between responsive and laggy touch as a quality judgement about the product, not as an understanding of hardware limits.

Creative Navy's documented design decisions for Elsner included exploring six navigation architectures before converging on a hamburger-plus-dashboard model, adding a user-configurable dashboard for most-used functions, aligning animation timing with firmware update intervals, and designing explicitly for sensor fault states, calibration drift, and delayed sensor readings. Touch targets were designed around the cited Colle & Hiszem (2004) ergonomics parameters: minimum 13mm, with accuracy plateauing at approximately 22mm.

bodySections.heading: Dealer and Distributor Networks Can Provide Market Feedback When Direct User Access Is Limited
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Dealer and distributor networks often mediate the relationship between manufacturer and end user in multi-market consumer products. Dealer feedback can function as a proxy for end-user insight in markets where direct research access is limited, but the evidence must be labelled as dealer evidence rather than treated as direct end-user research.

In the Elsner Elektronik case, dealer networks from 10 countries were involved in design validation. A 20-user survey was distributed and collected by Elsner, with Creative Navy analysing raw results. Formal usability testing involved 12 subjects in one structured session. Dealer prototype reviews produced 30 responses from dealers across 10 countries.

The Elsner dealer result is client-reported from Elsner's dealer network: 100% of responding dealers, 30 of 130 total dealers, rated the redesign as an improvement over the previous interface. The same evidence also records client-reported daily interaction frequency of approximately 25 interactions per day, client-reported early post-launch sales described as better than expected, and client-reported dealer promotion behaviour after launch.

The Streetec kntrl 2 case shows a different channel-mediated pattern. Dealers and installers mediate the manufacturer's relationship with owners, and the testing sample reflected that structure. After the design phase, two testing sessions were run with 32 participants total using the actual production product installed in a car: 13 in Munich, all tuning enthusiasts and car owners; and 19 at a trade fair in Spain, with a mixed sample of roughly 25% owners or enthusiasts, 40% dealers, 30% installers, and 5% other.

The Streetec trade fair sample should not be described as representative of owners. Its value is that dealers and installers commission and fit these systems. Creative Navy designed the test protocol, ran both sessions, and analysed the results. Streetec prepared the vehicle and site logistics and recruited participants. The supportable result is that all 32 participants completed all three tasks unassisted and performed in line with expectations.

bodySections.heading: Multi-Country Marketplaces Need Explicit Coherence Boundaries
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The OLX automotive marketplace case demonstrates market fragmentation in a multi-country consumer platform. OLX Group's automotive vertical operated across key markets including Poland, Portugal, and Romania. At the start of the engagement, local market teams had independently introduced their own filters, flows, and entry points across countries. The product was functionally different in each market.

The documented problem was feature bloat, late-cycle rework, and inability to run cross-market campaigns reliably. The central design tension was local market responsiveness versus global platform coherence.

The process included a three-day opening workshop in Lisbon with product, design, research, marketing, and engineering from key automotive markets. A shared end-to-end journey map was assembled across discovery, search, shortlisting, contact, negotiation, and post-sale, with known pain points and OLX data attached. Journey mapping covered first-time mobile-only buyers, experienced comparison shoppers, users moving between desktop and app, private sellers, and dealers.

Creative Navy's documented design decisions included a marketplace coherence framework: a small set of journeys consistent everywhere, including search-to-contact and listing creation, with explicitly defined points where countries could adapt modules, content, and copy. The work also included a brand-agnostic design system across iOS, Android, and mobile web, and a feature decommissioning practice in which every new feature proposal was paired with a decommissioning plan for the legacy flow it would replace.

The OLX outcome is a governance outcome, not a user performance outcome. Before the engagement, the boundary between fixed and adaptable did not exist as a documented, agreed framework. After the engagement, country teams could propose adaptations within defined limits, engineering had a stable reference, and marketing could plan cross-market campaigns. No user performance metrics were measured in this engagement.

bodySections.heading: Regulation, Units, and Market Defaults Can Become Product Architecture
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Multi-market consumer products may need architecture that reflects regulatory or market-specific requirements. A regulatory fact in one market can become a product-architecture fact for both markets when the same product must support multiple deployments.

Streetec kntrl 2, the second generation of Streetec GmbH's kntrl control system for aftermarket automotive air suspension, shows this pattern. CE rules require SI units, so bar is the European default. PSI is retained as a switchable option for the American market. The documented implication is that European and American unit divergence shaped the product architecture rather than remaining a simple label choice.

This distinction matters because market adaptation is not always content localisation. In Streetec's case, a regional regulatory requirement affected defaults and switchable units. In the OLX case, local differences affected filters, flows, modules, content, and copy. In Elsner's case, different markets were reached through dealer networks and validated through dealer prototype reviews.

bodySections.heading: Brand-Neutral Systems Support Products Whose Final Brand May Be Unknown to the Interface
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Brand-agnostic design systems are needed when one product architecture must support multiple brands or market variants. The requirement is not only visual substitution; the structure, layout, and component behaviour must remain coherent when colour, logo, language, or market-facing content changes.

AIT's heat pump controller demonstrates brand neutrality in an embedded product. The controller shipped and is in the market in a touch-only hardware configuration. The interface was delivered in three complete themes: two of AIT's consumer brands and a neutral OEM theme. Brand difference was confined to colour; structure, layout, and components were identical across all three.

AIT's stated position was that the interface should be neutral because AIT sells under two of its own brands and also has OEM customers with brands of their own. The sharper constraint was that units are produced brand-neutral and may not know their brand at first power-up, so the welcome screen cannot carry a logo at all.

The AIT controller also had 21 interface languages. It had no Fahrenheit, and no zoning: the controller holds one temperature per circuit, while room distribution is handled downstream by a separate room unit. These are engagement facts, not measured outcomes. No performance, efficiency, commissioning-time, error-rate, commercial figure, usability result, or comprehension result is stated for AIT, and nothing in that engagement was tested with users.

bodySections.heading: Language Variation Can Affect Component Layout and Interaction Logic
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Multi-market products often need interfaces that absorb languages the designer does not directly see during design. Language variation can change component choice, layout logic, and scanning or selection flows.

visioncheckout is a German vendor of computer-vision self-checkout systems for staff restaurants and catering. The product is in development; nothing has shipped and no outcome of any kind is claimed.

The documented deployment model includes closed-world sites with a known population and dual-language display, and open-world sites serving the public with a language selector offering English, German, French, Italian, and Spanish. Item names typically exist in only one language, while interface text must show two.

Customers apply their own logo and accent colour. The documented boundaries are that there is no customer-editable typography and no customer-editable component styling.

The dual-language constraints shaped component decisions. In the Corrector, sidebar category navigation was used because multi-row top-tab overflow grows too tall under dual language and obscures content when the bottom bar appears. QR scanning window placement followed layout logic rather than a fixed position because dual-language text length rules out centring where both keycard and QR options are shown.

visioncheckout pairs with AIT as a multi-brand and multi-language design problem. AIT had 21 languages and three brand themes; visioncheckout has deployment types, customer logos and accent colours, and language combinations the designer may not directly see. In both cases, interface architecture must absorb languages and brands without allowing component behaviour to fragment.

strongClaims: The Elsner Elektronik Cala Touch KNX work involved a 4-inch 480×480px room controller used across 54 countries, with a user base spanning building automation professionals and elderly consumers with limited dexterity.
The OLX automotive marketplace engagement produced a marketplace coherence framework defining consistent journeys and adaptation points, but no user performance metrics were measured.
Streetec kntrl 2 testing used the production product installed in a car with 32 participants; all 32 completed all three tasks unassisted and performed in line with expectations.
AIT's heat pump controller interface was delivered in three complete themes and 21 interface languages, with brand difference confined to colour and no user testing or performance outcome stated.

visioncheckout design constraints include dual-language display, a five-language selector for open-world sites, customer logo and accent colour, and layout decisions shaped by dual-language text length.
weakerClaims: Consumer and multi-market product design requires balancing local adaptation with shared product architecture across markets, languages, brands, units, and dealer networks.

Elsner dealer prototype reviews returned 30 responses from dealers across 10 countries, and 100% of responding dealers, 30 of 130 total dealers, rated the redesign as an improvement over the previous interface.
limitations: Elsner dealer review results are client-reported from Elsner's dealer network and apply to responding dealers, 30 of 130 total dealers.
OLX evidence supports a governance outcome and organisational capability, not measured user performance.
Streetec testing evidence must not be expanded into a completion percentage, task time, mean, or baseline comparison, and the trade fair sample must not be described as representative of owners.
AIT evidence is limited to engagement and shipped-product facts; no performance, efficiency, commissioning-time, error-rate, commercial, usability, or comprehension result is stated.
visioncheckout is in development; no shipped outcome, test result, compliance claim, certification credential, or commercial outcome is stated.
